title: Fruits of the Forest

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: After the poorest people of the Amazon allowed her to study their land and its ecology, Patricia Shanley turned her research findings into a picture book. The book is called Fruit Trees and Useful Plants in the Lives of Amazonians, but is better known simply as ‘the fruit book’. It has been so well received (and well used) that no less a dignitary than Brazil's environment minister has written the introduction

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Shanley's work on the book began over a decade ago, with a request for help from the Rural Workers' Union of the Brazilian town of Paragominas, whose prosperity is based on the timber trade. The union realised that logging companies would soon be approaching the peasant farmers living in the region. Isolated and illiterate, the farmers would have little concept of the true value of their trees, communities downstream had already sold off large blocks of forest for a pittance.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: The union wanted to know how valuable the forests were, and whether harvesting wild fruits would make economic sense there. There was a lot of interest in trading non-timber forest products (NTFPs), Shanley says. In a seminal paper published in the journal Nature in 1989, researchers had claimed that revenues from the sale of such products could far exceed those from the one-off sale of trees to loggers. ‘The union was keen to discover whether it made more sense to conserve the forest for subsistence use and the possible sale of fruit, animals and medicinal plants, than to sell trees for timber,’ says Shanley.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Working closely with the local farmers, Shanley and her team identified three trees in the region whose fruit was much favoured – bacuri, uxi and piquia. The farmers used their fruits and knew what sort of wildlife they attracted. But they had no measure of the trees' financial worth. ‘From a scientific point of view, hardly anything was known about these trees,’ she says. But six years of field research yielded a mass of information. During 1993 and 1994, 30 families weighed everything they used from the forest – game, fruit, fibre, medicinal plants – and documented its source.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: After three logging sales and a major fire in 1997, the researchers were also able to study the ecosystem’s reaction to logging and disturbance. This involved a similar, though less exhaustive, study which was carried out in 1999, this time with 15 families. The differences were striking. The average amount of forest fruit eaten in each household had fallen from 89 to 28 kilograms between 1993 and 1999. ‘What we found,’ says Shanley, ‘was that fruit collection could coexist with a certain amount of logging, but after the forest fires it dropped dramatically.’ Over the same period, fibre use also dropped from around 20 to 4 kilograms. The fire and logging also affected the nature of the farmers' diet. In 1993 most households ate game two or three times a month. By 1999 some were fortunate if they ate game more than two or three times a year.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Shanley's team also gathered data on game caught by local hunters, persuading local hunters to weigh their catch, and noting the trees under which the animals were caught. Over the year, hunters trapped five species of game averaging 232 kilograms under piquia trees. Under bacuri, they caught just two species averaging 63 kilograms; and under uxi, four species weighing 38 kilograms on average. At last, the team was getting an idea of which trees were worth keeping, and which could reasonably be sold. ‘This showed that selling piquia trees to loggers for a few dollars made little sense,’ explains Shanley. ‘Their local value lies in providing a prized fruit, as well as flowers which attract more game than any other species.’

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: As a result of these two studies, Shanley told the Rural Workers Union of Paragominas that the thesis as published in Nature could not be applied in its entirety to their community – harvesting NTFPs would not always yield more than timber sales. Fruiting patterns of trees such as uxi were unpredictable; for example, in 1994, one household collected 3654 uxi fruit, the following year: none at all. Geography was another factor preventing the farmers in the study from establishing a serious trade in wild fruit: villagers in remote areas could not compete with communities collecting fruit close to urban markets, although they could do some trade with passing river boats. This does not mean wild fruit trees are unimportant. On the contrary, argues Shanley, they are critical for subsistence, something often ignored in much of the current research on NTFPs, which tends to focus on their commercial potential.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: But Shanley and her colleagues decided to do more than just report their results to the union. After they had gathered the data, they held workshops for villagers interested in their findings. However, they soon realised they could only reach a small audience that way. And so they wrote the fruit book. The book has been remarkably influential, and is used by colleges, industries and the farmers themselves. Its success is largely due to the fact that people with poor literacy skills can understand much of the information it contains, thanks to its illustrations, anecdotes, stories and songs. ‘The book doesn't tell people what to do,’ says Shanley, ‘but it does provide them with choices.’ Farmers who have used the book now have a much better understanding of which trees to sell to the loggers, and which to protect.
